newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right say Jospin attracting more immigrants.
newsitem.headline: French right say Jospin attracting more immigrants.

text.p: Two leading Gaullists predicted on Wednesday that a plan by new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin to legalise thousands of illegal immigrants would attract more foreigners to France and bolster the extreme right.

"This absurd policy, applied in contempt of the law and republican values, carries the seeds of racism and xenophobia," said former interior minister Jean-Louis Debre, a leader of the Gaullist RPR party of President Jacques Chirac.
"You'll see. They'll soon be talking about granting foreigners the right to vote in French elections," Debre told the rightwing daily Le Figaro.
The policy shift was "a strong signal to all illegal immigrants that France is heading for a lax period", inviting a new flood into the country, RPR deputy Pierre Lellouche said on Radio Monte Carlo.

Keeping a campaign promise, Jospin on Tuesday ordered a case-by-case examination of tens of thousands of applications for legalisation. Many of them are from Africans who find themselves in a legal limbo because they can neither obtain residence rights nor be expelled for a variety of reasons.
It was unclear how many immigrants could win residence rights.

Those now eligible include parents of children born in France, spouses of immigrants with legal status, those in danger if sent home, patients receiving intensive medical care, students and immigrants "well-integrated in French society".
Illegal immigration is an emotional issue in France, where the extreme right National Front blames record 12.8 percent unemployment on the presence of too many foreigners.
An estimated five million foreigners live in France, of whom about one million, mostly Africans, are thought to be illegal.
Voters strongly supported the former centre-right majority when it tightened France's already tough immigration laws earlier this year, according to opinion polls.

Curiously, however, immigration barely surfaced as an issue during the May-June parliamentary elections, perhaps because the centre-right did not want to appear to be reaching out to National Front voters.
While the left generally welcomed Jospin's policy shift, some human rights groups offered only limited praise.

A group representing immigrants who last year occupied a Paris church and launched a hunger strike in protest at immigration requirements before being evicted by police, pledged "the struggle will continue" while it waited to see whether the new government keeps its word.
The human rights group "Droits Devant!" urged Jospin to do more by legalising all immigrants without papers, ending expulsions and undoing the immigration law reforms.

Both the right and the extreme-right predicted the new policy would drive rightist voters to abandon the mainstream rightwing parties in favour of the National Front, which advocates shipping home millions of immigrants and reserving jobs, education and social programmes for French natives.

The Front, which won nearly 15 percent of the vote in the first round of this year's parliamentary election, has proclaimed itself the only genuine opposition group in France and the new core of a restructured right wing.

"Forty thousand illegal immigrants legalised soon," said the pro-Front newspaper Minute in a banner headline. "Everything leads us to believe the National Front has not yet stopped growing, especially if the new government opens its doors to foreigners."
